exhibitors.name: Blumira
exhibitors.description: Cloud SIEM with EDR, ITDR and XDR plus 24/7 SecOps help for IT teams and MSPs; covers CJIS, NIST and CMMC compliance
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A cloud SIEM and detection-and-response product company that names local government and K-12 among the IT teams it sells to, so it is a govtech product vendor with a real SLED line.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
I tried to break this three ways and it holds.

(a) Supplier test: the precedent files manufacturers, distributors/resellers, field contractors, consultancies, guards and course providers as suppliers (DLT, Kurita, Allied Universal). Blumira is none of those — it is a first-party SaaS product company that builds and sells its own cloud SIEM/detection-and-response platform. Nothing in the row suggests it resells another vendor's stack, installs hardware, or delivers services/consulting. "Supplier" would be a misfile here.

(b) Sector/category test: the product is a security monitoring platform bought by IT teams, not by a fire chief, a public-works director, or a school transportation office. Of the valid options, General Gov > IT & AI Platforms is the only category that matches what the product actually does. There is no Cybersecurity category anywhere in the list, and K-12 Schools has no IT category (only School Safety, Transportation, Operations & SIS), so even though K-12 is a named buyer it cannot be placed there without distorting the category's meaning. General Gov / IT & AI Platforms is the correct home.

(c) Scope test: the strongest adversarial angle is that Blumira is a horizontal SMB/mid-market security vendor and public sector is just one of several industry pages. But the rules explicitly close that door — SLED can be enterprise, mid-market or SMB, and deal size and sales motion say nothing about scope. The row names local government and K-12 directly in the buyer field, focus is "Private primary with a SLED line", and it is neither federal-only nor defence-only. That is a real SLED line, and a SLED security salesperson would want to see these openings.

Board hygiene, though it is not the placement question: parent is null so there is no parent/sibling board risk, and the Greenhouse board currently shows 0 roles, so there is no huge-general-purpose-board trap either — an empty board, not a noisy one.

One honest caveat on strength rather than direction: the SLED evidence in the row is a single line ("Public sector named as an industry served"), which is industry-page-level evidence rather than proof of a dedicated public-sector sales team. That would justify a modest confidence rating on the SLED line, but it does not change the outcome, sector or category — vendor / General Gov / IT & AI Platforms is right on this row.

exhibitors.name: BOSS Solutions
exhibitors.description: Help desk/ITSM software (BOSSDesk) and 811 locate-ticket management (BOSS811, BOSSDig) for governments, utilities and schools
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: IT service management and help desk software (BOSSDesk) sold directly to cities, counties and universities - a govtech product company with a public-primary focus.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
I tried to break this three ways and could not.

(a) Supplier test: the row's own fields say offering="software/SaaS", sells="yes", and names a single owned product (BOSSDesk). That is not the shape of anything in the project's supplier precedent — no pipe/precast, no distribution or resale (DLT), no hardware sold through contractors (Kurita), no staffed service (Allied Universal), no consultancy or course provider. BOSS Solutions builds and licenses its own ITSM/help-desk platform, so it fails every supplier pattern and lands as a product vendor.

(b) Sector/category test: ITSM and help-desk ticketing is bought by the central IT department of a city, county, or campus — the exact thing "General Gov > IT & AI Platforms" exists to hold. The row's buyer list ("Government agencies, cities, counties and universities") is led by general-purpose local government, so General Gov beats Higher Education even though universities are named; Higher Education > IT & Administration would be the second-best home, not the right one, because it would strand the city/county majority of the buyer base. No other category is a candidate — this is not Citizen Services (no resident-facing transaction), not Finance & ERP, not Strategy & Performance.

(c) Horizontal-software objection: ITSM is a horizontal category and BOSS surely sells to private-sector IT shops too. But focus="Public primary" plus named public buyers is the standard the board uses, and a horizontal product with a public-primary go-to-market is still a vendor — the supplier bucket is for the wrong *kind* of company, not the wrong mix of customers.

Two cautions that do not change the placement:
- roles=0 and provider="careers page, no openings listed" — there is nothing to wire today, so wire_board should be false for the mechanical reason that the board is empty, not for the parent/noise reasons. No parent is listed (parent=null), so the parent's-board trap does not apply, and a small self-hosted careers page is the opposite of the huge-general-purpose-ATS trap.
- The flag is worth keeping visible: "Business Oriented Software Solutions Inc." collides with a USPTO contract-vehicle holder of the same legal name. Any future automated enrichment or board-wiring keyed on the legal name rather than the domain (boss-solutions.com) risks pulling federal contract data or postings that belong to the other entity. That is a data-hygiene note on the record, not a reason to re-place it.

exhibitors.name: Check Point Software Technologies Ltd.
exhibitors.description: Cybersecurity platform: network firewalls, cloud, email, endpoint and SASE security, plus threat intelligence, for enterprises and governments
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: Network, firewall and cloud security platform with government named among its customers - the same call the board already makes for Palo Alto Networks, Tanium, SentinelOne and Proofpoint.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
I tried to break this three ways and it held.

(a) The supplier test does not bite. The project files pipe/precast makers, distributors, resellers, field contractors, consultancies, course providers and guards as suppliers (DLT, Kurita, Allied Universal). Check Point is none of those - it is the first-party author of its own network, firewall and cloud security software, sold under its own name. The one angle with teeth is that Check Point also ships security gateway appliances, which could be dressed up as "equipment manufacturer", but the appliance is a form factor of its own software, and the board already seats Palo Alto Networks, which sells firewall hardware the same way, as a vendor. Heavy channel distribution does not convert the product company into a reseller either - the reseller in that precedent is DLT, not Check Point.

(b) Placement matches the actual product. Network, firewall and cloud security is IT infrastructure bought by a government's IT shop, not a Public Safety, Courts or Utilities line-of-business system. General Gov > IT & AI Platforms is exactly where the board already puts Tanium, SentinelOne and Proofpoint, so this is consistent rather than novel. No disqualifier applies: not federal-only, not defence-only, and "governments worldwide" is a named public buyer, so sells=yes stands.

(c) The one real weakness is about wiring, not about the outcome. The SLED evidence in the row is thin and generic - "Enterprises and governments worldwide" and "Government named among customers" name no state, county, city, district or campus buyer, and focus is "Mixed". That is enough to place the company by precedent but not enough to assume a SLED sales motion, so I would not push confidence above medium on this row alone.

Carrying that into board wiring: provider is "own page, no ATS detected" with 189 open roles at a global security vendor. Those 189 are overwhelmingly R&D, global enterprise sales and international support, not SLED sales - the huge general-purpose board trap. I would set wire_board=false and cite the 189 count rather than scrape a global careers page into a 6,405-posting board. Also flag the 2025-2026 acquisitions (Lakera, Veriti, Cyclops, Cyata, Rotate): no acquired-brand board should ever be wired as Check Point's, and no Check Point requisition should be reported under an acquired brand - the Rave/Motorola and RoadBotics/Michelin failure.

Verdict: vendor, General Gov > IT & AI Platforms is right on this row. The correction needed is wire_board=false plus verification of a real state/local/education sales motion before promoting it.

exhibitors.name: ControlAltProtect
exhibitors.description: Managed cybersecurity for small and mid-sized businesses: threat protection, detection, incident response and breach recovery
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: A managed security SERVICES provider, not a product company, and the row shows no live public-sector business to support a vendor call.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
The outcome is right and I could not refute it. "Managed security services" is a services practice, not a govtech product — the same bucket the project already uses for Allied Universal, DLT and the consultancies — so vendor is off the table, and it is a private company rather than an agency, association or brand, so not_a_company does not apply either. Supplier is the correct filing.

The sector is where the placement fails. General Gov has zero support anywhere in this row: buyer is "Businesses", focus is "Private primary", sells is "unclear", and nothing names a city, county, state or general-government buyer. The single public-sector thread in the entire row points the other way — a 2019 pitch to Houston County Schools (AL). Thin as that is, it is the only evidence of a public buyer type, and a supplier filing should follow the evidence rather than default to General Gov as a catch-all. That is exactly failure mode (b): parking a company in a sector its actual business shows no contact with. File it under K-12 Schools / Suppliers & Services.

Two cautions for the parent, both from the row itself. First, confidence here is low on any sector: one postponed pitch from seven years ago is not a public-sector practice, and a reviewer who preferred to treat the sector as genuinely undetermined would have a fair case — my correction is the best-supported option, not a strong one. Second, the flags say the About and Careers pages now 404. That is a signal the company may no longer be a live employer with a sales-hiring pipeline, so it is a poor promotion candidate regardless of sector, and nothing in this row supports wiring a job board for it.

exhibitors.name: CyberFOX
exhibitors.description: Privileged access, password management, DNS filtering, and SASE for MSPs and lean IT teams, with lines for K-12, higher ed, and local government
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: Privileged access and password management software - a product company, with public sector named among the verticals its MSP customers serve.
exhibitors.verifier_why: The vendor call rests on the wrong link in the chain. Per the row, CyberFOX's buyer is "MSPs serving SMB incl. local government" - its customer is the managed service provider, not the agency. That is the project's own supplier pattern: DLT the reseller was filed as a supplier, and the precedent explicitly covers a company whose buyers are intermediaries "with municipalities only as specifiers." An MSP is exactly that intermediary; local government appears here as a downstream end-customer of CyberFOX's customers, one vertical among the SMB verticals its partners serve. CyberFOX is certainly a product company (privileged access / password management software), but "product company" alone is not the vendor test - being a GOVTECH product company is, and PAM-for-MSPs is a horizontal SMB security tool with no public-sector-specific product, no agency procurement motion, and no named SLED buyer in the row. The supporting evidence is thin by the row's own admission: the sole justification is "Public sector named among MSP verticals," a mention on a verticals list, not a public customer, contract, or SLED sales team. The board exists so a salesperson can find SLED sales jobs; a CyberFOX rep sells channel/MSP partnerships, so the single open role would be mis-sold as a SLED seat. Filing it as General Gov > Suppliers & Services keeps it visible and promotable without asserting a govtech sales motion the row does not show. Secondary notes: the "focus" field's "Private primary with a SLED line" is unexplained anywhere else in the row and should not be leaned on; if it were kept as a vendor, IT & AI Platforms would at least be the right shelf for PAM software - my objection is the outcome, not the sector. One flag for whoever wires the board: the Jun 2026 Timus Networks acquisition means postings reached from cyberfox.com may now carry Timus or combined-group requisitions, so confirm the 1 role is CyberFOX's own before wiring.

Three things the parent should still act on, none of which change the outcome:

(a) DUPLICATE RECORD - /Users/wyethwest/govtech-dock/data/suppliers.json already holds id "rubrik" at General Gov > Suppliers & Services ("exhibited at MESC 2026", website null, "not researched"). exhibitors.name: Scale Computing, Inc.

exhibitors.is_govtech_why: It sells an edge computing and hyperconverged software platform with government and education named as verticals, which is a product company with a SLED line.

The offering is "software/SaaS" and the desc is a platform (edge computing / hyperconverged infrastructure) sold directly to the buyer's own IT shop - it is not a reseller (DLT), a process-hardware maker (Kurita), a contractor, a guard firm, or a consultancy, which is what every item in the project's supplier precedent actually is. sells=yes is supported by named public buyers (government and education), not inferred. On placement: an edge/HCI compute platform is bought by a county, city or district IT department, so General Gov > IT & AI Platforms is the right home, and no other valid category (Public Works, K-12 Operations & SIS, Utilities Broadband) matches what the product does - there is nowhere better to move it. Two live risks that do not change the outcome but should be recorded. (2) The flags are a wire_board problem, not a classification problem: Acumera (Peak Rock) acquired it Jul 2025 and took the Scale Computing name, and parent is listed as "Acumera / Peak Rock", so the paylocity board is very likely the combined entity's board carrying Acumera's own retail/convenience-store network roles. exhibitors.name: Secto (legal name Secto AI, Inc.)
exhibitors.description: Browser security for regulated teams: credential protection, Zero Trust enforcement, extension monitoring, Shadow AI governance, anti-phishing
exhibitors.is_govtech_why: It is an AI security operations software platform with government named as a buyer, so it is a product company, though the row never says state or local.
exhibitors.verifier_why:
The reviewer's own reason contains the refutation: "the row never says state or local." The only buyer evidence is "Government and enterprise security teams" — unqualified "government" alongside "enterprise," with focus recorded as "Mixed." Nothing in the row names a city, county, state, district, campus, or any public agency. An AI security-operations (SOC/detection-and-response) platform is the category of company most likely to be federal- and defence-led, and federal-only or defence-only disqualifies outright — so the single word "Government" is exactly the fact that needs checking, not the fact that settles it. "Why: Government named" is a keyword hit, not a SLED finding, and "unclear" is the honest read of this row.

On the two named failure modes: (a) does not apply — Secto is software/SaaS, not a manufacturer, distributor, reseller, contractor or consultancy, so the DLT/Kurita/Allied Universal supplier precedent is not the issue and I would not downgrade it to supplier. (b) is only conditionally fine — if Secto does sell to state and local, General Gov / IT & AI Platforms is the right home for a cyber platform, since there is no dedicated Cybersecurity category. The category is not the defect; the missing SLED predicate underneath it is.

Two further weaknesses in the row: provider is "not found" and roles is null, so there is no ATS and no evidence of any open sales requisition — nothing to wire and no sales-team signal to corroborate a go-to-market, consistent with a very early-stage startup. And the flag "NOT Secto Design (lighting)" shows the name is ambiguous, so any downstream enrichment on "Secto" carries a disambiguation risk.

Recommend holding rather than boarding. What would flip it to vendor: a named state, county, city, school district, university or other SLED customer/case study, or a public-sector page that says state and local rather than just "government." What would kill it: evidence the public-sector business is federal/DoD/IC only. Confidence in the current placement, on this row alone: low.
